1c4wdyt: At the neighborhood market, a lot of small bags were thrown away at the end of each morning. An association proposed banning them immediately, but several vendors pointed out that some people needed to separate wet products. Since they didn't want to replace one problem with another, they began by observing when the bags were used and what alternatives were possible.
hrsguw: The final campaign combined three measures. They put up a sign so customers would remember to bring containers, offered reused boxes for large purchases, and set aside bags for products that really needed them. A week before the start, they explained the changes at each stall. They didn't do it to give a perfect image of the market, but to reduce one specific kind of waste without making shopping harder for those with fewer options.
10pnlez: After a month they counted how many bags had been handed out and asked vendors and customers what had worked. Use had dropped, although some signs weren't well understood. They decided to add drawings and place them before the checkout area. The campaign did not solve all of the neighborhood's environmental problems; it made it possible to test a small change and improve it. For its organizers, that result was more useful than announcing a big transformation without explaining what each person should do on arriving at the market.
